title: The Brain Controls the Body
keyIdea: Your brain is the boss of your body. It sits inside your head, safe under a hard skull. Your senses (eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin) notice things and send messages along thin nerves to your brain. The brain thinks and decides what to do. Then it sends messages along nerves to your muscles, and they move. Eyes see a ball, the brain decides to catch it, and nerves tell your hands to move. Your brain never switches off: even when you sleep, it keeps you breathing and warm.
familyTip: Play catch with a soft ball. Each time, say the three steps out loud: my eyes see it, my brain decides, my hands catch. Then try with eyes shut and notice how much harder it is when your eyes cannot send the message.

visual.caption: Does this part notice things or move you? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the boss, send sense messages up nerves, order sense, brain and muscles, and see the brain at night.

kid: Your brain is the boss of your body. It is inside your head. A hard skull keeps it safe, like a helmet. Your brain thinks, feels and remembers. It also tells every part of you what to do.
Your senses help the brain. Eyes see. Ears hear. Your nose smells. Your tongue tastes. Your skin feels. Each sense sends a message to the brain along thin wires called nerves.
The brain gets the message and decides what to do. Then it sends a message down the nerves to your muscles. The muscles move. Eyes see a ball. The brain says catch it. Your hands move and catch.
Messages on nerves are very fast. Some go faster than a car on a big road. Your brain works all the time, even at night. While you sleep, it keeps you breathing and warm, and it makes dreams.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. This topic sits in the animals including humans strand of the National Curriculum in England (Year 1: identify the parts of the body and say which part goes with each sense) and links to NGSS 1-LS1-1 and 4-LS1-2, where animals take in information through their senses, process it in the brain and respond. The model taught is the simple loop used in KS1 and early KS2 resources: senses (receptors) send messages along sensory nerves to the brain, the brain decides, and motor nerves carry messages to muscles (effectors).

The lab has five tasks. Learners tap a body to find the boss, then send five sense messages up the nerves to the brain. They put two short stories into sense, brain, muscles order. They drag a message from the brain down the nerves to the leg, arm or face to do a job. Last, they pick what the brain still does at night: breathing, keeping warm and dreaming. Fast nerve messages travel at up to about 100 metres per second, which is faster than a car on a motorway.

Common mistakes. Young children often say the heart does the thinking, or that hands and feet move by themselves. Some think messages travel in the blood, or that the brain switches off at night. Take care with reflexes: pulling a hand away from something hot is a fast reflex through the spinal cord, so this lesson uses caught balls and called names as its brain examples, not hot objects.

practice.hint: Think of the part with a hard skull, like a helmet.
practice.explain: Your brain is inside your head. The hard skull keeps it safe.

practice.prompt: You have 5 senses. You have used {n} of them today. How many more can you try?
practice.hint: Start at 5 and take away the senses you used.
practice.explain: 5 − {n} = {=5-n}. Eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin make 5 senses.

practice.prompt: You smell a cake. Which sense sends the message to your brain?
practice.hint: Which part of your face do you sniff with?
practice.explain: Your nose smells. It sends a message along nerves to your brain.

practice.prompt: Sam's brain sends {a} messages to wave and then {b} messages to kick. How many messages is that?
practice.hint: Add the waving messages and the kicking messages.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} messages. Each one zooms along nerves to the muscles.

practice.prompt: Your hand catches a ball. What happened first?
practice.hint: A sense notices first, then the brain decides, then muscles move.
practice.explain: Eyes see the ball first. Then the brain decides to catch, and nerves tell the hand to move.

pool.prompt: What is the boss of your body?
pool.explain: The brain is the boss. The heart pumps blood and the tummy breaks up food.

pool.prompt: What carries messages from your brain to your muscles?
pool.hint: They are like thin wires all through your body.
pool.explain: Nerves carry messages. Blood carries food and air, and bones hold you up.

pool.prompt: A dog barks {n} times. Each bark sends 1 message from your ears to your brain. How many messages?
pool.hint: One bark makes one message, so count the barks.
pool.explain: {n} barks make {n} messages from your ears to your brain.

pool.prompt: Mia says her legs decide to walk all by themselves. What is right?
choices: Her brain tells her legs to walk
Her eyes tell her legs to walk
pool.hint: Think about which part of the body is the boss.
pool.explain: Legs do not decide. The brain sends a message along nerves to the leg muscles.

pool.prompt: What does your brain do when you are asleep?
pool.hint: Do you stop breathing when you sleep?
pool.explain: Your brain never switches off. Asleep, it keeps you breathing and warm, and it makes dreams.

pool.prompt: You blink {a} times, then {b} more times. Each blink needs a message from the brain. How many messages?
pool.hint: Add the first blinks and the next blinks.

pool.prompt: A lemon tastes sour. Which sense tells your brain?
pool.hint: Which part do you taste with?
pool.explain: Your tongue tastes. It sends the message to your brain along nerves.

pool.hint: It is hard, like a helmet.
pool.explain: The skull is hard bone around the brain. Hair is soft and only keeps you warm.

choices: Sense notices, brain decides, muscles move
Muscles move, brain decides, sense notices
Brain decides, muscles move, sense notices
pool.hint: What has to happen before the brain can decide?
pool.explain: A sense notices first and tells the brain. The brain decides. Then nerves tell muscles to move.
